title: Death (CCC 1005–1014)

cards: Ash Wednesday. A line shuffles toward the front of the church: office workers on a lunch break, kids in school uniforms, an old man with a cane.

One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb of gray ash onto each forehead, in the shape of a cross, and says a sentence nobody would put on a greeting card: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.
Nobody is required to come. The line still reaches the back door. Why would Catholics want that reminder?

teach.b: The words are God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In Latin, memento, homo, quia pulvis es: remember, human, that you are dust.
That word memento, remember, gives today's phrase: memento mori, remember that you will die. The Catechism is honest about death.

It's the end of earthly life, and it's natural, and in Christian teaching it's also a consequence of sin, something God did not originally want for human beings. But Christ, it says, has changed its meaning.

teach.h: A PASSAGE, NOT ONLY AN END.
teach.b: Because he died and rose, Catholics say, death is no longer only an end. It can be a passage. Paul could write to the Philippians of "having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ."
And tradition says that Francis of Assisi, near his own death, added a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising God for our Sister Death. So why remember it? Not to be morbid.
The Catechism says remembering death reminds people that their time to make something of their lives is limited.
The old litany of the saints even asks to be spared a sudden and unprepared death: not to be spared death, but to meet it ready.

Remembering changes a Tuesday: the grudge looks smaller, the phone call to your mother looks bigger. Old paintings of saints at prayer sometimes put a skull on the desk, beside the book and the candle. Not fear.

how: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with the words remember that you are dust, pray for a holy death, and many keep November as a month of remembering the dead.

o: a warning that your own death is coming soon
a Latin prayer asking to be spared from death
remember that you will die, so you live well

practice: Imagine, gently, the day people gather to remember you: not the sad part, just the words.
What would you want someone who loved you to say, not your job title, but something like she always had time, he made people laugh, they never gave up on anyone?
Let one sentence come and hold it; if you pray, you can ask for help to become it.

wordCard.voice: Memento mori. Latin for remember that you will die: an old Christian practice of keeping death in view, not out of fear, but to live well. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: remember that you will die (literally, remember to die).

carryVoice: Your line: remember you will die. Ash Wednesday says it once a year; your line can say it any day. See you tomorrow.
